one_liner: MuseScore's engraving library compiled to WebAssembly; a no-layout metadata mode claims 3x over MuseScore's native batch converter.
what_it_does: Runs MuseScore's core library (libmscore, built from MuseScore 4.0 since webmscore 1.0.0) in browsers (inside a Web Worker) and in Node.js (in-process), as the npm package webmscore. You load MSCZ/MSCX, MusicXML, MIDI or Guitar Pro data with WebMscore.load(format, data, fonts, doLayout) and call async methods such as saveSvg, savePdf, saveMidi, saveXml, saveAudio, metadata/saveMetadata and measure or segment positions. It replaces spawning the MuseScore desktop binary for conversions, not a C++ API.
how_it_is_fast: There is no speed technique in the code: the release build uses -Oz (size optimisation) through Emscripten and Qt5 for WebAssembly. The claimed 3x comes from Boost Mode (doLayout=false), which loads the score with updates locked and never runs layout, so metadata or MIDI export skips the engraving pass, and from reusing one warm in-process instance instead of a batch run of the desktop program.
when_to_use: Extracting metadata (title, parts, measures, key and time signatures, tempo, lyrics) from many MuseScore files in Node.js or a browser without installing MuseScore: use Boost Mode.
Rendering MuseScore scores to SVG, PNG, PDF, MIDI or audio inside a web page or PWA, where shipping the desktop program is not possible.
Server-side conversion pipelines pinned to Node 16 that can accept GPL-3.0 code.
when_not_to_use: You need PDF or sheet images fast: Boost Mode cannot produce PDF, and with layout enabled the README gives no speed comparison against native MuseScore.
You need MusicXML or MXL from Boost Mode: the benchmark script notes saveXml and saveMxl 'cannot work properly' without layout.
Long batch jobs: open issue #13 reports a bus error after thousands of load/saveMidi/destroy cycles in one Node process (10 files work), with no reply.

Current Node.js or recent MuseScore 4 files: issue #12 says it only works on Node 16 (ERR_INVALID_URL on 18 and 20; a member blamed an upstream undici bug in April 2024, no fix), and issue #14 (Sep 2024) reports blank output for recent MuseScore 4 files, unanswered.
Proprietary or permissively licensed products: GPL-3.0 as a MuseScore fork.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond the bundled wasm and data files (webmscore.lib.wasm about 7.4 MB plus webmscore.lib.mem.wasm about 3.9 MB as of 0.22.0); extra fonts (e.g. @librescore/fonts) for CJK text; an sf2/sf3 soundfont for audio; building from source needs Emscripten 2.0.6 and patched Qt5 5.15.2 for WebAssembly
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js 16 in practice (README says v8.9.0+, issue #12 says 18 and 20 fail); browsers Chrome 57, Firefox 53, Edge 16, Safari 11
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly runtime: browsers (Web Worker wrapper) and Node.js (in-process)
integration.thread_safety: Single global wasm instance with process-wide state (current project, one shared soundfont file); in browsers calls are serialised through one Web Worker; scores must be freed with destroy()
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces 'musescore -j' conversions with a JavaScript API (one call per output), not the command line or job file

gotchas: Harness flaw: web-example/benchmark.js times load(doLayout=false) plus saveMetadata in a warm in-process wasm instance, returning a string in memory, against 'musescore3 -j' doing full layout and writing 200 .metajson files to disk, with process teardown inside the timed span; the 3x measures skipped layout and I/O, not WebAssembly beating native code, and no timings, hardware or MuseScore version were published.

The two sides do not produce the same output: metaJson writes json["pages"] = score->npages(), which only layout fills, so Boost Mode metadata most likely reports 0 pages where MuseScore's batch converter reports the real count (read in src/converter/internal/compat/notationmeta.cpp and web/main.cpp, not run).

The claim is stale: benchmark.js was last changed on 2020-05-31 ('feat: boost mode, 3x faster than the musescore software', webmscore 0.7.0, MuseScore 3 based) and still spawns musescore3, while webmscore 1.0.0 (2023-01-13) was rebuilt on MuseScore 4.0; the current release has never been measured.
Without extra fonts, characters outside the bundled FreeFont render as tofu in SVG/PNG/PDF; CJK fonts are not bundled since 0.6.0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling handles music notation; pick webmscore when the job is reading or rendering MuseScore files in a browser or Node, the way DuckDB-Wasm or Essentia.js bring their native C++ engines to the web, and accept that its speed claim rests on skipping layout rather than on faster code.
verified_claims_summary: The README says Boost Mode is about 3x faster than MuseScore's '-j' batch converter, from web-example/benchmark.js: 200 rounds of loading Aequale_No_1.mscz without layout and calling saveMetadata in Node, against one 'musescore3 -j' run converting 200 copies to .metajson with layout, first-file time subtracted. No per-run numbers, hardware, Node or MuseScore version are given, and the measurement dates from webmscore 0.7.0 (May 2020).
status_note: Stale: last commit and npm release 1.2.1 on 2023-01-24, 12 open issues with no fixes since (Node 18+ broken, recent MuseScore 4 files give blank output, bus error in long batches); GPL-3.0, copyable only into GPL-compatible projects.
